faq.a: Yes, subarachnoid haemorrhage, severe dehydration, or spinal pathology can produce a positive sign.
faq.q: Can Kernig's sign be positive in non‑infectious conditions?

faq.a: No; it lowers suspicion but does not exclude meningitis, especially early or in immunosuppressed patients.
faq.q: Is a negative Kernig's sign reassuring?

faq.a: Start empirical antibiotics after blood cultures and arrange transfer for imaging or LP when possible.
faq.q: What if I cannot perform a lumbar puncture?

exam: A 4‑year‑old with fever and neck stiffness: which bedside sign do you perform first and why? — Kernig's sign; it is quick, bedside, and suggests meningitis.
Patient has a positive Kernig's sign but normal CT head: what is your next step? — Obtain blood cultures, start empirical antibiotics, and arrange lumbar puncture.
How does HIV infection change your differential for a positive Kernig's sign? — Raises likelihood of TB or cryptococcal meningitis; add anti‑TB drugs or antifungal therapy if indicated.
Why is dexamethasone given before antibiotics in bacterial meningitis? — Reduces inflammatory cytokine surge, decreasing risk of hearing loss and neurological sequelae.
You cannot obtain a CT scan; the patient is obtunded with a positive Kernig's sign. What do you do? — Proceed with LP only if no focal signs; otherwise treat empirically and arrange urgent transfer.
Distinguish Kernig's from Brudzinski's sign in terms of patient movement. — Kernig's: hip flexed, extend knee; Brudzinski's: passive neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion.

What are the key CSF findings in bacterial versus tuberculous meningitis? — Bacterial: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein; TB: lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein, positive acid‑fast stain.
Explain why aminoglycosides are avoided in meningitis therapy. — Poor CSF penetration; they cannot achieve therapeutic levels in the subarachnoid space.
ai.title: Kernig's Sign
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Kernig's sign is a bedside maneuver indicating meningeal irritation, most commonly due to meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage. It helps clinicians differentiate infectious from non‑infectious causes of headache and fever in low‑resource settings.

b: Positive sign = resistance or pain on knee extension
Negative sign = smooth knee extension without discomfort
sections.p: Kernig's sign is elicited with the patient supine, hip flexed to 90°, then the knee is extended. Pain or resistance at >30° knee extension suggests meningeal irritation.

b: Common in bacterial meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage
Less specific in severe dehydration, severe neck pain, or spinal pathology
sections.p: Meningeal irritation occurs when the pia‑arachnoid membrane is inflamed, causing painful stretch of the nerve roots during hip/knee movement.

b: Positive sign → start empirical meningitis treatment (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin) after blood cultures
Consider TB meningitis in HIV‑positive or chronic cases; add rifampicin‑based regimen
If trauma history → suspect subarachnoid bleed; arrange urgent CT if available
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, Kernig's sign guides urgent decisions when lumbar puncture or imaging are delayed.

b: Describe exact patient position and angle of hip/knee
Explain why a positive sign points to meningitis over simple headache
State next immediate step: blood cultures, start antibiotics, arrange LP if safe
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to perform, interpret, and act on Kernig's sign in a realistic scenario.

t.b: Confirms meningitis type; CSF cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, PCR for TB/cryptococcus
Excludes mass effect before LP; looks for subarachnoid bleed
Identify bloodstream pathogen before antibiotics; guides targeted therapy
Detects immunosuppression that raises TB or cryptococcal risk

b: Empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) – chosen for broad coverage, avoid aminoglycosides due to poor CSF penetration
Add dexamethasone before first antibiotic dose to reduce inflammation and hearing loss
If TB meningitis suspected → start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol; avoid fluoroquinolones early due to resistance concerns
Maintain airway, give IV fluids, monitor vitals, treat seizures if present
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause while providing supportive care.

b: Brudzinski's neck flexion sign – neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion
Jolt accentuation – worsening headache with rapid head rotation
sections.p: Other meningeal signs can be mistaken for Kernig's sign.

b: Early bacterial meningitis may have normal signs
Severe neck pain from cervical spondylosis can mimic a positive sign
sections.p: A negative Kernig's sign does not rule out meningitis, especially early in disease or in immunocompromised patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Altered consciousness, seizures, or focal neurological deficit with a positive Kernig's sign
Rapidly worsening headache and fever in a child or immunocompromised adult
